argument: Spinoza's life has to be understood against a backdrop of ferocious political and religious violence, exemplified by the mob murder of Johan De Witt, which shows that tribalism rather than religion itself is the deeper source of atrocity. Spinoza embodied a stubborn commitment to reason in this dangerous world: he refused a bribe to stay quiet about his heterodox views on God, was excommunicated for it, and later demolished a former friend's plea to convert to Christianity with arguments grounded in geometric certainty. That same danger of expressing unpopular ideas is why he never published his masterwork, Ethics, during his lifetime.
keyIdeas: The mob killing of Johan De Witt, done for political rather than religious reasons, is used to argue that religion is not the unique cause of atrocity — the deeper cause is humanity's tendency to form tribes and marginalize outsiders.
Spinoza's landlord locked him inside his house on the night of the massacre to stop him from posting a sign denouncing the mob, likely saving his life.

Offered a large bribe to stay silent about his views, Spinoza instead sent the Jewish authorities a rigorously structured, mathematical outline of his beliefs, which led to his formal excommunication.

In his reply to Albert Burgh, Spinoza claims to know his philosophy is true with the same certainty as a geometric proof, and argues that Christianity's rapid spread among common people proves nothing, since the same reasoning would support any group preaching in Christ's name.

Spinoza traces Burgh's devotion to the Church not to love of God but to fear of hell, which he calls the single cause of superstition; the same climate of danger that killed De Witt is why Spinoza withheld Ethics from publication until after his death.
